questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is in the passive voice?

options.text: The council repaired the flooded road.
The flooded road was repaired by the council.
The council is repairing the flooded road.
The council will repair the flooded road.

questions.explanation: A passive sentence has a form of *be* followed by a past participle, and its subject receives the action rather than performing it. In option b the road is the subject but the council still does the repairing, and *was repaired* is the tell-tale be-plus-participle pattern.

distractorRationale.a: The subject *council* performs the action, so this is active
distractorRationale.c: *Is repairing* is active continuous, not passive; the participle would be *repaired*
distractorRationale.d: *Will repair* is active future

questions.stem: Change to the passive voice: "The goalkeeper saved the penalty."

options.text: The penalty saved by the goalkeeper.
The penalty was saved by the goalkeeper.
The penalty is saving by the goalkeeper.
The penalty had saved the goalkeeper.

questions.explanation: Move the object *the penalty* to the front, insert the correct form of *be* in the original tense — simple past, so *was* — add the past participle *saved*, and put the original subject after *by*. That gives "The penalty was saved by the goalkeeper."

distractorRationale.a: Omits the auxiliary *was*, leaving a fragment with no finite verb
distractorRationale.c: Uses the -ing form instead of the past participle
distractorRationale.d: Reverses the meaning so that the penalty acts on the goalkeeper

questions.stem: Change to the passive voice, keeping the person as the subject: "The school awarded Amina a scholarship."

options.text: A scholarship was awarded Amina by the school.
Amina was awarded a scholarship by the school.
Amina awarded a scholarship by the school.
Amina has been awarding a scholarship by the school.

questions.explanation: When a verb has both a direct and an indirect object, either one can become the subject of the passive. The question asks for the person, so the indirect object *Amina* moves to the front, giving "Amina was awarded a scholarship by the school."

distractorRationale.a: Grammatically possible but makes the scholarship the subject, not the person the question asked for
distractorRationale.c: Omits the auxiliary *was*, so there is no finite verb
distractorRationale.d: Uses the active continuous form and reverses who gives and who receives

questions.stem: Change to the passive voice: "The Ministry has approved the new syllabus."

options.text: The new syllabus was approved by the Ministry.
The new syllabus has been approved by the Ministry.
The new syllabus has approved by the Ministry.
The new syllabus is approving by the Ministry.

questions.explanation: The tense of the original must be preserved. *Has approved* is present perfect, and the present perfect passive is *has been* plus the past participle, giving "has been approved". Changing the tense would change the meaning, so option a is not an acceptable answer.

distractorRationale.a: Shifts the tense from present perfect to simple past
distractorRationale.c: Omits *been*, so the verb is left in the active perfect form
distractorRationale.d: Uses the -ing form and the wrong tense

questions.stem: Change to the passive voice: "You must submit the completed form before Friday."

options.text: The completed form must submit before Friday.
The completed form must be submitted before Friday.
The completed form must been submitted before Friday.
The completed form is must submitted before Friday.

questions.explanation: A modal verb such as *must*, *can* or *should* stays exactly where it is, and the passive is formed by adding *be* plus the past participle after it: *must be submitted*. Notice that the vague agent *you* is simply dropped, which is one of the main reasons the passive is used in official writing.

distractorRationale.a: Leaves the verb active, so the form appears to do the submitting
distractorRationale.c: Uses *been* instead of *be* after a modal
distractorRationale.d: Inserts *is* before the modal, which English does not allow

questions.stem: In which situation is the passive voice the better choice?

options.text: When you want to make the doer of the action prominent
When the doer is unknown, unimportant or deliberately not named
When you want the sentence to be as short as possible
When the verb has no object at all

questions.explanation: The passive lets you talk about an action without naming who performed it, which suits reports where the doer is unknown — "The shop was burgled last night" — and scientific writing where the procedure matters more than the person: "The mixture was heated for ten minutes".

distractorRationale.a: That is precisely what the active voice does best
distractorRationale.c: The passive is normally longer, because it adds a form of *be* and often a *by* phrase
distractorRationale.d: Only verbs that take an object can be made passive at all

questions.stem: An intransitive verb such as *sleep* can be changed into the passive voice.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. The passive works by promoting the object to subject position, so a verb with no object has nothing to promote. "The baby slept" cannot become a passive sentence, which is why only transitive verbs have a passive form.

questions.stem: Change to the passive voice: "Who wrote this anonymous letter?"

options.text: Who was this anonymous letter written?
By whom was this anonymous letter written?
Whom wrote this anonymous letter by?
This anonymous letter was written by who?

questions.explanation: When the subject of an active question is *who*, the passive version puts it into the objective case after the preposition *by*, giving *By whom*. The object *this anonymous letter* then becomes the subject, and the verb becomes *was written*.

distractorRationale.a: Drops the preposition *by*, so the question no longer identifies an agent
distractorRationale.c: Leaves the verb active and strands *by* at the end ungrammatically
distractorRationale.d: Keeps the subjective *who* after a preposition, where *whom* is required in formal English

questions.stem: Change to the active voice: "The stolen motorcycle was recovered by the vigilante group."

options.text: The vigilante group recovered the stolen motorcycle.
The vigilante group was recovering the stolen motorcycle.
The stolen motorcycle recovered the vigilante group.
The vigilante group has recovered the stolen motorcycle.

questions.explanation: To go back to the active, make the agent after *by* the subject, drop *by* and the form of *be*, and put the verb in the tense the passive carried. *Was recovered* is simple past, so the active verb is *recovered*.

distractorRationale.b: Changes the tense to past continuous, which the original did not express
distractorRationale.c: Swaps the roles so that the motorcycle performs the recovery
distractorRationale.d: Changes simple past into present perfect

questions.stem: A student writes in a laboratory report: "I poured the acid into the beaker and then I heated the mixture." Which revision suits the register of a formal scientific report?

options.text: I poured the acid into the beaker and heated the mixture.
The acid was poured into the beaker and the mixture was then heated.
The acid, I poured into the beaker, and the mixture I heated.
Pour the acid into the beaker and heat the mixture.

questions.explanation: Scientific reports describe what was done rather than who did it, so the passive is the conventional choice: the procedure becomes the focus and the experimenter disappears. Option b converts both verbs to the passive while keeping the sequence of events clear.

distractorRationale.a: Tidier than the original but still first-person active, which formal reports avoid
distractorRationale.c: An awkward inversion that is neither passive nor natural English
distractorRationale.d: Turns the report into instructions for someone else to follow, changing the purpose of the writing

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is in the active voice?

options.text: The book was read by the students.
The cake was baked by my mother.
The teacher explains the lesson.
The homework was completed by the class.

questions.explanation: The sentence 'The teacher explains the lesson.' is in the active voice because the subject (the teacher) performs the action (explains). In contrast, the other sentences have the subject receiving the action.

distractorRationale.a: This sentence is passive; the action is performed on the subject.
distractorRationale.b: This sentence is passive; it indicates that the subject receives the action.
distractorRationale.d: This sentence is also passive; the class is not performing the action.

questions.stem: When is the passive voice preferred over the active voice?

options.text: When the doer is unknown.
When the action is more important than the doer.
When writing in first person.

distractorRationale.a: While true, it does not encompass all reasons for using passive voice.
distractorRationale.b: This is correct, but it is not the only reason.
